Meanwhile, every database team eventually discovers that identical queries waste effort; the same rows get read repeatedly while disks and network links stay busy. A cache sits between the application and storage, holding recent results so common requests return quickly.

However, a cache introduces its own hazards. Stale entries can serve outdated values after rows change, and invalidation logic grows tangled over time; a cached price that lags behind a real update can cost money. Teams must decide how long each entry lives, which keys to evict, and how to warm the cache after restarts.

Along with such risks, a good plan pays off. Hot data stays in RAM; cold data waits on disk until a call asks for it. Timing limits and LRU policy work as a pair, and monitoring hit ratios shows which parts of an app profit most from this approach.

Finally, treat the cache as a tool rather than a cure. Measure carefully, invalidate promptly, and call the work done.
